etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift: /ariɡataku/ → /ariɡatau/ → /ariɡatoː/.
From ありがたく (arigataku), the adverbial form of Old Japanese and Classical Japanese adjective ありがたし (arigatashi, modern ありがたい arigatai, “grateful, thankful; welcome”), from 有り (ari, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, continuative or stem form) of verb 有る aru, “to exist, to be”) +‎ 難し (katashi, “hard, difficult”, 難い katai in modern Japanese). The katashi changes to gatashi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
Modern Japanese -i adjectives formerly ended in -ki for the attributive form. This medial /k/ dropped out during the Muromachi period, both for the attributive form (-ki becoming -i) and for the adverbial form (-ku becoming -u). However, the adverbial form reverted to -ku thereafter for most words, with the -u ending persisting in certain everyday set expressions, such as arigatō, おはよう (ohayō), or おめでとう (omedetō), and in hyper-formal speech.
Arigatashi is first attested in the oldest literature of the 8th century. It originally meant “difficult to exist, hard to be”, shifting to “rare, special”, and then to “welcome, thankful, nice to have” by some time in the 15th century. This sense is still in use:
この天(てん)気(き)はありがたいね。 ― Kono tenki wa arigatai ne. ― This weather sure is welcome (literally, “This weather sure is hard to come by”)
The similarity to Portuguese obrigado (“thank you”) is purely coincidental; the Portuguese first arrived in Japan in 1543, well over a century after citations expressing gratitude are found.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from German Arbeit (“work, job”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English curry, from Tamil கறி (kaṟi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Dutch glas. Doublet of グラス.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Dutch kop and also from Portuguese copo. Doublet (via Late Latin cuppa) of カップ (kappu), from English cup.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of コンセントリックプラグ (konsentorikku puragu), wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism) derived from concentric +‎ plug, used since the late Meiji period. Sometimes the source word is mistaken for the unrelated English consent, which would be transliterated the same way.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki.
Although often described as wasei eigo (和製英語), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man, which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “salary man” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century.
The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー (sararī) +‎ マン (-man).
The term began to be used in the Taishō period and became firmly established by the early Shōwa period. Prior to its popularization, terms such as 月給取り, 俸給生活者, and 勤め人 were used for similar workers, alongside more derogatory terms like 腰弁当 and 洋服細民. Around 1960, the term ビジネスマン (bijinesuman) also started being used to avoid the mediocre image associated with this word.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Etymology tree
Arabic جُبَّة (jubba)bor.
Old Italian giubbabor.
Middle French jupe
Proto-Indo-European *-ōder.
Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.?
Latin -ō
Frankishinflu.
Old French -on
Middle French -on
Middle French jupon
French juponbor.
Japanese ズボン
Borrowed from French jupon (“petticoat, underskirt”), from French jupe (“skirt”), from old Italian jupa, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”). Doublet of 襦袢.
Note that the meaning has changed from “underskirt” to “trousers/pants”, and the second consonant has changed from /p/ to /b/, possibly influenced by native Japanese onomatopoeia ずぼん (zubon), describing the action of something sliding into place, as when one puts on or takes off trousers.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-der.?
Latin pānem
Old Galician-Portuguese pan
Portuguese pãobor.
Japanese パン
From Portuguese pão (“bread”), from Latin pānem, accusative singular form of pānis (“bread”). Compare French pain, Italian pane, Romanian pâine, Spanish pan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English pan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Πάν (Pán). (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowing from Dutch bier.
First cited to a text from 1724 with the kanji spelling 麦酒 (literally “barley liquor”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Portuguese botão; compare English button.
First attested in 1651.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, ボタン (botan), is the katakana spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from English mansion. The term gained currency in the latter half of the 1950s, used to lend an air of luxury to high-density residential development projects.
Note that while English mansion most commonly means “large house”, it is also occasionally used to mean “luxurious apartment”, and this latter usage was borrowed into Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt-
Proto-Germanic *hwītaz
Proto-West Germanic *hwīt
Old English hwīt
Middle English whit

Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der.?

Japanese ホワイトシャツ (howaito shatsu)
Japanese ワイシャツ<tr:waishatsu>
Clipping of ホワイトシャツ (howaito shatsu), borrowed from English white shirt, from the typical white color of dress shirts.
The meaning in Japanese evolved over time to extend first to any dress shirt, regardless of color, and then to any long-sleeved button-down shirt in general.
First cited to 1912. Natsume Sōseki uses the term in his 1915 book 道草 (Michikusa, “Grass on the Wayside”) with the spelling 白襯衣 (literally “white + shirt”), using furigana to indicate a pronunciation of ワイシャツ (waishatsu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 此 (ke, “this”) +‎ 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The initial /ke/ is an alternative form of the initial /ko/ (此, “this”) seen in words such as ここ (koko, “this place → here”) or これ (kore, “this [nominal] → this”), and the final /sa/ is a contraction from */ke.asa/ to /kesa/ with the medial -a- falling out, as Old Japanese did not permit vowel clusters.
It is the same element found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/konteu/ → /kontjoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 今朝 (MC kim trjew, literally “now morning”). The /eu/ → /joː/ sound shift is a regular phonological change.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
兄弟 on Japanese Wikipedia
From 兄 (kyō, “elder brother”, goon) +‎ 弟 (dai, “younger brother”, goon), from Middle Chinese 兄弟.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 兄 (kei, “elder brother”, kan'on) +‎ 弟 (tei, “younger brother”, kan'on), from Chinese 兄弟. Compare 兄妹 (keimai, “elder brother and younger sister”), 姉弟 (shitei, “elder sister and younger brother”), and 姉妹 (shimai, “elder and younger sisters”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 先生 (MC sen sraeng, literally “born earlier”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
出(で)る (deru, “to exit”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “opening, door”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From 切(きっ)符(ぷ) (kippu, “a ticket used for public transport”) + 手(て)形(がた) (tegata, “commercial paper”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 切手, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 刺(さ)し (sashi, “sticking into, sticking between; slicing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu, “to stick into”)) + 身(み) (mi, “flesh, meat”). The use of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu) here to mean slice is irregular, and may be due to the kill connotations of the verb 切(き)る (kiru, “to cut, to slice”) during the Muromachi period when the word sashimi first appears.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 友(とも) (tomo, “friend”) + 達(たち) (-tachi, pluralizing suffix). Originally plural, but also used in the singular sense in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in Japanese in 1900 in the katakana form タイフーン (taifūn), itself a borrowing from English typhoon.
Prior to the Meiji era (1868–1912), this kind of severe storm was called a 野分き (nowaki), literally a "field-splitter" for the way the winds would wreak havoc on farms. The term タイフーン (taifūn) then appears in 1900, also attested with spelling 大風 and reading of taifun. Then in 1907 meteorologist Okada Takematsu (岡田武松) scientifically defined what qualifies as this specific type of storm, and then purportedly as phono-semantic matching of the English typhoon, adopted the kyūjitai kanji spelling 颱風 (read as taifū without that final "n") on the basis of Chinese references using the term 颱風 / 台风 (táifēng). This spelling then became common from the Taisho era (1912–1926).
There was likely some influence from Chinese on the form of the Japanese word. In Walter Henry Medhurst's English and Chinese Dictionary of 1847-48, he glossed the English word typhoon as Chinese 太風 / 太风 and 颶風 / 飓风 (jùfēng), the former of which would be read in Japanese as taifū.
The origins of English typhoon are somewhat uncertain, with possible ancient connections to Chinese. See that entry for more.
台 is a daiyōji replacing 颱.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
By surface analysis, 哲(てつ) (tetsu, “clear, wise, sage”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “study”). Coined by Nishi Amane in his 1874 百一新論 as a translation of English philosophy or Dutch filosofie. Nishi's kanji spelling 希哲學 (hirosohi) is literally calqued from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía, “pursuit of wisdom”, literally “love of knowledge”), apparently from the Chinese morphemes 希 (xī, “to long for”) and 哲 (zhé, “wisdom”), before he later settled with 哲學 (modernly spelt 哲学).
Nishi also used the transcriptions ヒロソヒ, ヒロソヒー (hirosohī) and 斐鹵蘇比.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably a compound of 宮 (miya, “shrine”) +‎ 笥 (ke, “small box”).
The ke changes to ge as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Superficially of 土(ど) (do, “land, ground”) + 産(さん) (san, “production, produce”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/di t͡ɕin/ → /d͡ʑiɕiɴ/
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese compound 地震 (MC dijH tsyinH). First cited to a text from 734.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /nai/
From Old Japanese. First cited to 720 in the Nihon Shoki.
Apparently this term semantically first referred to the ground, and was used most in constructions like ないふる (naifuru, “the ground shakes”). Over time, this shifted via metonymy to refer to the shaking itself.
May be a compound of 土(な) (na, “ground”, possibly an apophonic form of ni, "earth, soil") + 居(ゐ) (i, “being”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of 居(ゐ)る (iru, “to be”, in a location; in modern Japanese, used of animate objects)).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /naje/ → /nae/
Appears in the Nippo Jisho.
Shift from nai, historical nawi (see above). First cited to the late 1400s.
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compound of 地 (ji, “ground”) +‎ 震い (furui, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical Japanese verb 震ふ (furufu, “to tremble; to roar”), related to modern 震える (furueru)). The furui changes to burui as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨i me2⟩ → */jiməɨ/ → /jɨme/ → /jume/
Shift from Old Japanese 夢 (ime2), itself a compound of 寝 (i, “sleep, sleeping”, obsolete) +‎ 目 (me, “eye; sight, vision”).
Appears in texts from the 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 夢 (MC mjuwngH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Literary Chinese, possibly early Mandarin 蒲團／蒲团 (pútuán), likely as part of the importation of Zen Buddhism, for which practice these were originally used. First cited in Japanese to a text from the early-mid 1200s with the "meditation cushion" sense.
Originally referred literally to a 蒲 (pú, “bulrush, cattail”) 團／团 (tuán, “ball”), from the way these were round cushions made from woven bulrush leaves.
After the term was borrowed, the usage and construction of these cushions changed and the connection with bulrushes was weakened, leading to the simpler character 布 (fu, “cloth”) being used as a replacement for 蒲 (fu, “bulrush, cattail”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 恋(こい) (koi, “love”) + 人(ひと) (-hito, “person”). The hito changes to bito as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 伝う (tsutau, “to go along something (intransitive); to move something along, to transmit something (transitive)”).
The expected form of such a compound would be either てつたう (tetsutau), or てづたう (tezutau) with rendaku. The actual attested form of てつだう (tetsudau) suggests metathesis, with the voicing of rendaku shifting from the tsu to the following ta.
First attested in the late 1500s in 狂言 (kyōgen, “popular plays”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 紙 (kami, “paper”). The kami changes to gami as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
An etymologically unrelated false friend of Chinese 手紙 / 手纸 (shǒuzhǐ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/teɡami/ → /teɡaɴ/
Shift from standard Japanese tegami, dropping the final vowel and keeping the nasal.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/arataɕi/ → /ataraɕi/ → /ataraɕiki/ → /ataraɕiː/
In Old Japanese, the original term was 新たし (aratashi), composed of older 新た (arata, “new”) + adjective-forming suffix し (shi). This persisted until at least the mid-1200s, and indeed the adjective stem arata is both modern adjective 新た (arata, -na adjective) and the root of verbs such as 改める (aratameru, “to renew, refresh, revise, or reform something”). See 新た (arata) for further details of that etymology.
Starting from the 900s, the aratashi reading began shifting to atarashi. This metathesis may have been due to conflation with 可惜し (atarashi, “magnificent, excellent, precious; regrettable”). The aratashi reading then became more and more uncommon in Early Middle Japanese, and the “new, modern, fresh” sense became the main use, superseding the largely homophonous 可惜し (atarashi) and pushing it out of common usage.
The modern form is from Early Middle Japanese adjective 新(あたら)し (atarashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii).
Displaced Old Japanese 新し (nipisi, adjective). This is reflected in the modern language as prefixing stem 新 (nii-), which is no longer productive.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Shift in meaning from 朝 (ashita, “next morning”), itself cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is from Chinese 明日 (míngrì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE).
Various theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
Possibly a shift from verb 明かす (akasu, “to pass”).
*/akasu/ → */akusu/ → /asu/
Possibly an apophonic form of or cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 明日.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/mʲau nʲiti/ → /mʲɔːɲit͡ɕi/ → /mʲoːɲit͡ɕi/
From Middle Chinese compound 明日 (MC mjaeng nyit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From a later borrowing of Chinese 明日 (míngrì), using the 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”).
Rare reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 土圭 (tʰuoX kwei, literally “earth, clay + stack of clay tablets”, a kind of sundial used in the Zhou Dynasty).
The 土圭 spelling is the original form, with the kan'on reading of tokei. This has been largely superseded by the spelling 時計 in modern writing, which uses the 時 character as ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Probably this spelling from native Japanese word ときはかり(see below). Alternatively, the kanji spelling could be interpreted as jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), using the meanings of the characters as 時 (“time”) + 計 (“measurement”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 時(とき) (toki, “time”) + 計(はか)り (hakari, “measuring”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 計(はか)る (hakaru, “to measure”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Derived from 気(け)色(しき) (keshiki).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 景色 (MC kjaengX srik).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
果物 on Japanese Wikipedia
果物 (kudamono, kabutsu): various kinds of fruit.
Literally “tree's thing”. Originally a compound of 木 (ku, “tree”, irregular shift from ancient ko pronunciation) +‎ だ (da, possessive marker between two nouns, only found in a few compounds) +‎ 物 (mono, “thing”).
The medial da is also seen in 獣 (kedamono, “beast”, literally “hairy thing”). The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/kwabut͡su/ → /kabut͡su/
Possibly from Middle Chinese compound 果物 (*kuɑ *miuət, literally “fruit thing”). Compare modern Mandarin 果物 reading guǒwù (rare), Cantonese gwo2 mat6 (rare).
Rarely used in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
桜 (sakura): the Japanese cherry tree, Prunus serrulata
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:サクラ
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Prunus serrulata
Wikipedia
English Wikipedia has an article on:Cherry blossom
Wikipedia
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki, the oldest extant historical record of ancient Japan, compiled in 712 CE.
Originally derived from 咲く (saku, “to bloom, burst open”) +‎ 等 (-ra, nominalizing and pluralizing suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/au/ → /ɔː/ → /oː/
From Middle Chinese 櫻 (MC 'eang).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:梅雨
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:East Asian rainy season
Wikipedia
First attested in the mid-Muromachi period.
Derivation unclear, likely theories include:
May be cognate with 露 (tsuyu, “dew, dewdrop”), from the way the rainy season causes everything to be covered in drops that may look like dew. However, the pitch accent differs, as 露 (tsuyu) has either an 頭高型 (atamadaka-gata) or 尾高型 (odaka-gata) pattern, while 梅雨 (tsuyu) has a 平板型 (heiban-gata) pattern.
Alternatively, may be cognate with classical verb 熟ゆ (tsuyu, modern 熟える (tsueru), “to become ripe”), as plums ripen during the rainy season. In light of the pitch accent and semantics, this derivation appears more likely.
The spelling is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 梅雨.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 梅雨 (MC mwoj hjuX), in poetic reference to the season when plums grow or ripen.
Alternatively, the 黴雨 spelling may have been the original spelling. This is homophonous in Middle Chinese, and literally means “mold + rain”, in reference to how moldy things get during this season of constant humidity.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨tano1siki1⟩ → */tanʷosikʲi/ → /tanoshii/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. No Ryukyuan cognates exist; as a result, further derivation unknown. Theories include:
A compound of 手 (ta, “hand”, combining form) + 伸す (nosu, “to extend”)
This is problematic, as nosu has first been attested starting from the early 900s, with no A/B distinction (see Jōdai Tokushu Kanazukai for details).
From 田神 (tano, literally “rice paddy god”)
No reading of 神 (*no, “god”) exists.
A borrowing from an unknown language
No words resemble *tanV meaning "fun" or "to enjoy".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of 湯帷子 (yukatabira).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Old Japanese 火事 (pi2 no2 ko2to2) (now spelled as 火の事 (hi no koto)), later read with 音読み (on'yomi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/winaka/ → /inaka/
Possibly a compound of 居 (i, the 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete form”) and 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem form”) of verb 居る (iru), “to be, exist (of animate objects)”) +‎ 中 (naka, “inside, middle”).
The spelling is from Chinese 田舍 (tiánshè).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
(This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium.)
Also read with rendaku (連濁), as denja.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From 畳む (tatamu, “to fold”, verb).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 疊 (dep, “to fold”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 皮肉 (MC bje nyuwk), literally “skin and meat”.
Originally a Buddhist term from the Zen expression 皮肉骨髄 (“skin, flesh, bones, and marrow”) used to evaluate disciples’ understanding, where “bones and marrow” represent the core truth, and “skin and meat” symbolize the superficial understanding.
As a result, it came to refer to shallow criticism (pointing out faults without addressing the essence) and irony in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 真(ま)っ (ma'-, “true, pure”) + 赤(あか) (aka, “red”).
First cited to the mid-1400s.
The outright sense arose from the way that something purely red is obvious and clearly visible.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:眼鏡
Wikipedia ja
眼鏡 (megane, gankyō): a pair of eyeglasses.
Probably originally a compound of 目 (me, “eye”) +‎ 金 (kane, “metal”, in reference to the metal used in eyeglass frames). The kane changes to gane as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The spelling is based on an apparent borrowing from Chinese, see the gankyō reading below.
Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/ɡankjau/ → /ɡankjɔː/ → /ɡankjoː/
Probably a borrowing from written Chinese 眼鏡 / 眼镜 (yǎnjìng). Eyeglasses are first mentioned in Chinese in the 1400s as 靉靆 / 叆叇 (aidai?), a transcription of an Arabic term. By the late Ming dynasty, eyeglasses appear in writing as 靉靆即眼鏡 / 叆叇即眼镜 (“aidai, i.e. eye-lenses”), using the compound term 眼鏡 / 眼镜 (yǎnjìng, literally “eye + lens”). Compare modern Min Nan reading gán-kiàⁿ.
This reading appears in texts from the 1920s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 着(き) (ki, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 着(き)る (kiru, “to wear clothing”)) + 物(もの) (-mono, “thing”). Compare the similar formation of the word 食(た)べ物(もの) (tabemono, “food”, literally “eating thing”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE in the ideographic spelling 裳, later attested less ambiguously in the Utsubo Monogatari of the late 900s CE.
As contact with the West grew, the sense shifted from referring generically to any clothing to referring specifically to 和服(わふく) (wafuku, “(traditional) Japanese clothing”), in particular kimono and other robe-like full-length garments (長着(ながぎ) (nagagi)), as opposed to Western apparel (洋服(ようふく) (yōfuku)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 社會 (MC dzyaeX hwajH, “public gathering for offering to the god of earth”), as a compound composed of 社 (dzyaeX, “god of earth; ceremony for offering to the god of earth”) + 會 (“gathering”). The word was repurposed by Fukuchi Gen'ichirō in 1875 to translate the western concept of society.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/kʷaɡaku/ → /kaɡaku/
First attested in the mid-Meiji period as a translation of English science.
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived elements 科(か) (ka, “field, imperial examination, compounding the radical 斗 (“measuring tool”)”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “school, study”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: As 科(か)学(がく) (kagaku) above has become homophonous with 化(か)学(がく) (kagaku, “chemistry”), 科学 is sometimes read as 科(しな)学(がく) (shinagaku) to differentiate. However, reading 化学 as 化(ばけ)学(がく) (bakegaku) is more common.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Maeno Ryōtaku in 1777.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 經濟 (keng tsejH), short for 經世濟民 (“to administer the state to relieve the suffering of the people”), through its use as a translation of English economics by Japanese scholars during the Meiji period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Likely from Dutch kan (“cylindrical metallic container”), with additional influence from English can (“cylindrical metallic container”). The kanji is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Alternatively, from Middle Chinese 罐 (kuɑnH, “can; jar; tin”). The usage of 缶 is likely due to a 新字体 (shinjitai) simplification from earlier 旧字体 (kyūjitai) 罐, where the phonetic component 雚 was entirely eliminated.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 缶, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally from 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 美しい (ishii, “good; delicious”, possibly obsolete in modern contexts; the delicious sense evolved out of 女房詞 (nyōbo kotoba, “women's word”) usage).

etymologies.text:

Coined in Japan in 1870 in the Meiji period in reference to a patented tricycle design. Later used to refer to bicycles.
Compound of Sinitic-derived elements 自 (ji, “self”) +‎ 転 (ten, “rolling”, simplified modern form of 轉) +‎ 車 (sha, “vehicle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 花(はな) (hana, “flower”) + 火(ひ) (hi, “fire”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Not attested until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573), as a shortening of older 蕎麦 (soba mugi, literally “soba grain”).
Two theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation of the soba element:
Samuel Martin reconstructs soba as Proto-Japonic *sonpa and derives it as a compound of *so (unknown) +‎ *pa (“feather”). The *pa changes to *nba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
From 稜 (soba, “an edge, a corner”), in reference to the seed of the plant being a triangular oval shape with protruding corners.
Considering the late appearance of soba in isolation with the meaning of buckwheat, and the attested earlier senses of side; corner, edge, Martin's reconstruction seems unlikely.
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from 蕎 (“buckwheat”) +‎ 麦 (“wheat”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested as the ideographic spelling 蕎麦 in a section of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 722. Later attested in the 本草和名 (Honzō Wamyō, “Main Plants Japanese Names”, a Japanese reference of plants used in Chinese medicine, compiled in 918) with the phonetic spelling 曾波牟岐 (so pa mu gi).
Analyzable as a compound of 蕎 (soba, “buckwheat”) +‎ 麦 (mugi, “dry-field grain”). However, the soba portion is not attested in isolation to mean "buckwheat" until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573). It appears that soba was originally the word 稜 (soba, “corner, angle”) in reference to the angular shape of the buckwheat grain. Compare the similar derivation of English buckwheat, where the buck element is cognate with beech and refers to the angular shape of the beechnut. An old Japanese name for the beech tree is in fact 柧棱木 (soba no ki), again in reference to the angular shape of the beechnut.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/sobamuɡi/ → /somamuɡi/
Shift in pronunciation from sobamugi. First attested in the early 1100s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
Possibly a borrowing from Middle Chinese 蕎麥 (MC kjew|gjew meak). First attested in a section of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 722, and additionally later in imported works written in Chinese by Bai Juyi (772–846).
Unclear if this reading was ever prevalent; use might have been limited to kanbun contexts. Not listed in many Japanese dictionaries.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of へ (he, “separate”) + 屋(や) (ya, “roof; house”). The へ (he) is related to the first element in 隔(へだ)たる (hedataru, “to be apart, to be separated”). First attested in the late 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 都合 (MC tu kòp, “to sum up; altogether”). First attested in Japan in the 正倉院文書 (Shōsōin Monjo) of 734 CE in the literal sense of “totaling” or “summing up.”
Over time, the meaning shifted from the “total sum of things” to the “general state of affairs” (circumstances) in the Middle Japanese period, eventually leading to the modern sense of “convenience.”

etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 明(あ)ける (akeru, “to dawn”) and 空(あ)ける (akeru, “to empty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Wasei kango, created as a translation of English telephone. Coined in Japanese as a compound of Chinese-derived 電 (den, “electric”) +‎ 話 (wa, “talking”). See also 話す (hanasu, “to talk, to chat”).
First attested in a text from 1891.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From 風(かぜ) (kaze, “wind”).
The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from Chinese 風邪 / 风邪 (fēngxié).
First attested in 984.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 風邪 (MC pjuwng zjae).
